title: Tokenization & Data Representation
description: Study byte-pair encoding, wordpiece and sentencepiece distinctions, vocabulary size and efficiency, and special tokens and chat serialization. Each lesson includes a worked example and an applied practice task.

lessons.title: Byte-pair encoding
lessons.description: Compare token counts for ordinary prose, a long identifier, and a non-English sentence using one fixed tokenizer.
lessons.conceptOverview: Byte-pair encoding builds larger token units through merge rules. Runtime tokenization applies a fixed vocabulary and merge procedure; it does not retrain on each input. The resulting token boundaries affect sequence length, rare strings, and multilingual efficiency.
lessons.whyItMatters: A deployed tokenizer applies its existing vocabulary and merge rules.

lessons.title: WordPiece and SentencePiece distinctions
lessons.description: Create a comparison table separating tokenization algorithm, normalization, vocabulary, and special tokens.
lessons.conceptOverview: WordPiece describes a subword modeling approach, while SentencePiece is a tokenizer toolkit supporting approaches such as unigram and BPE. Tokenizer normalization and whitespace handling are part of the model interface. Tokenizers are not interchangeable simply because vocabulary sizes match.

lessons.title: Vocabulary size and efficiency
lessons.description: Compare characters per token across two languages and explain the impact on context and cost.
lessons.conceptOverview: Larger vocabularies may shorten sequences but increase embedding and output-layer costs. The useful tradeoff depends on language coverage, data distribution, and architecture. Measure both tokenized length and model cost rather than optimizing vocabulary size in isolation.
lessons.whyItMatters: Vocabulary design trades sequence efficiency against representation and output costs.

lessons.title: Special tokens and chat serialization
lessons.description: Inspect a serialized conversation and label user, assistant, and end-of-turn boundaries.
lessons.conceptOverview: Chat models consume serialized token sequences, not abstract role objects. Role boundaries, assistant prefixes, and end-of-turn markers influence behavior. Use the checkpoint's intended chat template and avoid duplicating special tokens when composing messages.
lessons.whyItMatters: Use the model's expected serialization and special-token convention.
